text:
|| Hitopadesha ||

->|| 140 ||<-

"If war is at hand, O King, why is it not decided upon beforehand?" For it is said: What kind of servant or minister is he who, without consideration, advises the King to prepare for battle and abandon his own post at the very outset? Furthermore: One should strive to conquer enemies through means other than war, for in a battle between two parties, the outcome is never certain. Moreover: One should strive to overcome the enemy through <term>sama</term> <gloss>conciliation</gloss>, <term>dana</term> <gloss>gift/bribery</gloss>, or <term>bheda</term> <gloss>division</gloss>, either collectively or individually, but never by war. Furthermore: Everyone is a hero so long as he has not faced a conflict, and who is not arrogant when they have not yet seen the power of the opponent? Moreover: Nothing is as dangerous to living beings as war. Success obtained through small means is not a fruit of great value. Rather, seeing that war is present, one should treat it with disdain. For:

The <term>Chakravaka</term> <gloss>a bird, used here as a proper name</gloss> says: O Great King, war should not be practiced first, since he is neither a servant nor a minister who, without judging, advises the King to prepare for battle at the start and to abandon one's own position. Furthermore, one should try to conquer the opponent by means of conciliation and the like, and never by conflict, because it is not known for certain which of the two fighting parties will win. Moreover, one should try to resolve the enemy by conciliation, bribery, or division, either individually or together, and never by war. Besides, every person is a hero before a war is actually fought, because...

<summary>The text discusses the strategic dangers of entering into war prematurely and advocates for using diplomacy, bribery, and internal division to resolve conflicts instead.</summary>
<keywords>Hitopadesha, war, diplomacy, statecraft, Chakravaka, conflict resolution</keywords>
